questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which information is generally required to open a brokerage account?

choices.text: A credit card number and its security code
A copy of your last tax refund check
Social Security number, date of birth, address, and employment details
Your high school transcript and test scores

questions.correct_answer: Social Security number, date of birth, address, and employment details
questions.intro: Brokerage firms must verify your identity and learn about your situation. Applications usually ask for name, address, date of birth, Social Security number (or other taxpayer ID), employment information, and investment experience and goals.
questions.feedback: Identity and financial profile information are standard on brokerage applications.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Leo, 16, wants to invest. Most brokerage firms require individual account owners to be adults. Which option fits his age?

choices.text: A custodial account managed by an adult for Leo
An individual account opened in Leo's name alone
Using a parent's individual account without telling them
Waiting until age 30, the minimum to invest

questions.correct_answer: A custodial account managed by an adult for Leo
questions.intro: Minors generally cannot open individual brokerage accounts. A custodial account (often under the UTMA or UGMA laws) is opened by an adult custodian for a minor; the assets belong to the minor and are transferred to them at the age set by state law.
questions.feedback: Custodial accounts let adults invest on a minor's behalf.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Ana links her checking account and transfers $500 to her new brokerage account. What has she done?

choices.text: Bought $500 of stock automatically
Bought a $500 savings bond
Paid a $500 fee to open the account
Funded the account; she has not bought any investment yet

questions.correct_answer: Funded the account; she has not bought any investment yet
questions.intro: Funding means moving money into the account, often by an electronic transfer from a bank. After funding, the money sits as cash until you place an order to buy an investment.
questions.feedback: Moving money in is funding; buying requires a separate order.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Ana's brokerage account shows $500 in "cash" and $0 in investments. What should she do to invest?

choices.text: Nothing; the cash is invested automatically
Choose an investment and place a buy order
Transfer the money back to checking
Call the FDIC to activate investing

questions.correct_answer: Choose an investment and place a buy order
questions.intro: Investing requires choosing a specific investment (such as a fund) and placing an order. Many accounts leave deposited money in cash until you do.
questions.feedback: Cash stays cash until she places an order.

questions.feedback: A transfer moves your own money.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Settlement is when ownership and money officially change hands. For most stock trades the standard is "T+1." What does that mean?

choices.text: The trade takes one year
The trade settles one business day after the trade date
The trade can be reversed for one day
The trade costs $1

questions.correct_answer: The trade settles one business day after the trade date
questions.intro: The standard settlement cycle for most U.S. stock trades became T+1 (trade date plus one business day) in May 2024.
questions.feedback: T+1 = settlement one business day after the trade.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: In a custodial account for Leo, who owns the investments?

choices.text: Leo, though an adult manages them until he reaches the age set by law
The adult custodian forever
The brokerage firm
The state government

questions.correct_answer: Leo, though an adult manages them until he reaches the age set by law
questions.intro: Assets in a UTMA/UGMA custodial account legally belong to the minor. The custodian manages them for the minor's benefit until the age set by state law.
questions.feedback: The minor owns the assets; the custodian manages them.

questions.prompt: Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule is called dollar-cost averaging. What happens when prices are low?

The investor must wait for prices to recover

questions.feedback: $25 buys more shares at lower prices.
